skills.title: Components
skills.summary: Reusable, composable UI components and their lifecycle

concepts.title: Inputs down, outputs up
concepts.summary: Parents bind data into a child's inputs; the child reports changes through outputs instead of writing to its inputs

choices: `count.set` can only be called from `ngOnInit`
Templates can't call methods inside a `(click)` binding
An `input()` signal is read-only; the parent owns the value, so emit an output
The input must be marked `{ required: true }` before it can change
variants.explain: `input()` gives the child a read-only signal with no `set`. Declare an output such as `increment = output<void>()` and let the parent update its own state, or use `model()` for a two-way binding.

variants.q: In an Angular app, a `SearchBox` child needs to tell its parent page that the user typed a new query, so the page can refetch results. What is the usual design?
choices: The child injects the parent component and sets its field directly
The child declares an output like `queryChange`; the parent binds `(queryChange)`
The child writes the query to a global variable that the parent polls
The child reloads the whole page with the query string attached
variants.explain: An output lets the child announce what happened while the parent decides what to do. Injecting the parent ties the child to one specific parent and hides the data flow.

variants.q: A `Modal` gets `isOpen` as an input from its parent. To support its close button, the modal copies `isOpen` into its own signal and sets that to `false` on close. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing, as long as the modal has a close animation
The modal closes and the parent's value updates to match
The parent still holds `true`, so the modal can't be reopened
Angular merges the two values on the next change detection
variants.explain: Two owners of one value drift apart: the parent never learned the modal closed, so setting `true` again isn't a change. The parent should own `isOpen` and react to a `closed` output (or use `model()`).

concepts.title: Composition with content projection
concepts.summary: Building flexible components by projecting content in with `<ng-content>` instead of adding an input per variation

variants.q: A `Card` component has grown the inputs `showIcon`, `iconName`, `title`, `subtitle`, `showFooter`, `footerText` and `footerButtonLabel`, and every new screen needs another one. What is the usual refactor?
choices: Group all of the options into a single `config` object input
Move the options into global CSS classes that callers can toggle
Copy the component once per screen so each copy stays simple
Let callers project body and footer content with `<ng-content>`
variants.explain: Content projection lets the caller decide what goes inside, so the component stays small and stops growing an input for each case. A `config` object just moves the same flags into one place.

variants.q: Which design makes a `Dialog` component easiest to reuse across many different screens?
choices: `Dialog` projects a title, body and actions supplied by the caller
`Dialog` imports every screen's form and picks one using a `type` input
Each screen keeps its own copy of the dialog's markup and styles
`Dialog` looks up which content to show in a global store
variants.explain: When the caller supplies the content, the dialog handles only the shared behaviour (overlay, focus, closing) and needs no change for new screens. A `type` switch means editing the dialog every time a new use appears.

concepts.title: Who owns a form field's value
concepts.summary: One-way `[value]`, two-way `[(ngModel)]` or a reactive `FormControl`: which one holds the field's current value

choices: Both show `Grace`: `[value]` writes typed text back to the signal
The input shows `Grace`; the paragraph still says `Hello Ada`
Both show `Ada`: the input snaps back on every keystroke
Neither renders: `[value]` on an input needs `FormsModule`
variants.explain: `[value]` is a one-way property binding: it sets the DOM value when `name()` changes, and nothing listens for typing. Write back with `[(ngModel)]`, a `FormControl`, or an `(input)` handler that calls `name.set`.

choices: Disabled controls are reset to `null` when the form is read
`value` only includes controls the user has touched
Controls created from an object need `setValue` before they're read
`value` leaves out disabled controls; `getRawValue()` includes them
variants.explain: A reactive form's `value` holds only enabled controls, which suits forms where disabled means not applicable. When disabled fields should still be sent, read `getRawValue()`.

concepts.title: `track` in `@for`
concepts.summary: Giving `@for` a stable `track` expression so Angular keeps each item's DOM and component state with the right item

choices: `@for` rebuilds every row from scratch, so typed text is lost
Tracking by `$index` ties each row's state to its position, so it shifts
`track` needs a string, so `$index` is silently ignored
`app-todo-row` needs `OnPush` change detection to keep its state
variants.explain: After removing item 0, the row at position 0 is kept and handed the second todo, along with the first row's typed text. Track by a stable ID such as `track todo.id`.

variants.q: A list is refetched from the API every 30 seconds, which returns fresh objects each time. Which `track` expression fits best?
choices: `track $index`
`track item`, the object itself
`track item.updatedAt`
`track item.id`
variants.explain: A track key should be unique and stay the same for the same item. Refetched objects are new references, so tracking by object recreates every row; `$index` follows position; a timestamp changes on edit and may repeat.

variants.q: In Angular's built-in `@for` block, what happens if you leave out the `track` expression?
choices: Angular falls back to tracking items by object identity
The template fails to compile: `track` is required
Angular falls back to tracking by index, with a console warning
The loop renders once and ignores later changes to the list
variants.explain: Unlike the older `*ngFor`, where `trackBy` was optional, `@for` makes `track` mandatory so every loop chooses its item identity on purpose.

concepts.title: Cleaning up when a component is destroyed
concepts.summary: Ending subscriptions, timers and listeners with `takeUntilDestroyed`, `DestroyRef` or an effect's `onCleanup`

choices: Each old page's subscription is still alive after the page is destroyed
Angular runs component constructors twice in development mode
Root services are created again on every navigation
`messages$` replays every message to each new subscriber
variants.explain: Destroying a component doesn't end subscriptions it opened on a longer-lived observable. Pipe through `takeUntilDestroyed()` (the constructor is an injection context) or unsubscribe in a `DestroyRef.onDestroy` callback.

choices: Nothing: Angular clears timers started inside an effect
The effect runs only once, so the new delay is ignored
`setInterval` isn't allowed inside an `effect`
Intervals pile up, because the old ones are never cleared
variants.explain: The effect reruns when `delayMs()` changes but knows nothing about the timer. Register a cleanup: `effect((onCleanup) => { const id = setInterval(...); onCleanup(() => clearInterval(id)); })`. It runs before the next run and on destroy.

concepts.title: Derived state with `computed()`
concepts.summary: Deriving values from inputs and signals with `computed()` instead of copying them into extra state

choices: The new value, since input changes rerun `ngOnInit`
The first value: `ngOnInit` runs once, so the copy never updates
The new value, but one change detection cycle late
Nothing: Angular throws when a required input is copied
variants.explain: `ngOnInit` runs once per instance, so the copy is frozen at the first value. Read `initialPrice()` directly, or derive with `price = computed(() => this.initialPrice())`.

variants.q: A component keeps `fullName` in a signal and sets it from an `effect` whenever the `first` or `last` signals change. What is the simpler, more reliable approach?
choices: Set `fullName` in `ngAfterViewInit` instead of an effect
Assign `fullName` once as a plain field in the constructor
`fullName = computed(() => this.first() + ' ' + this.last())`
Move `fullName` into a root service that both fields write to
variants.explain: A value that can be computed from other signals shouldn't be its own state. `computed()` is always in step with its sources and recalculates only when they change; syncing with an effect adds a second copy that can lag.

concepts.title: Route component reuse
concepts.summary: Navigating between URLs of the same route keeps the component instance, so it must follow changing params

choices: The `snapshot` is cached for the whole session after the first read
`routerLink` skips navigation when only a parameter changes
The router reuses the component, so `ngOnInit` doesn't run again
Route params must be read with `params`, not `paramMap`
variants.explain: By default the router keeps the same component when only params change. Subscribe to `route.paramMap` (it emits each change), or bind the param to an input with `withComponentInputBinding()`.

variants.q: The router has `withComponentInputBinding()`, and `ProfilePage` declares `id = input.required<string>()` and loads the user in an `effect` that reads `id()`. The user has a half-typed note in a local signal. What happens on `/users/1` → `/users/2`?
choices: A new instance is created, so the note is cleared
Nothing: route inputs are set once, when the component is created
The router throws, since inputs can't hold route params
Same instance: `id` becomes `'2'`, the effect reruns, the note stays
variants.explain: The reused component gets its input updated, so anything derived from `id()` follows. Other local state is not reset, so per-user state must be cleared or derived from `id()` explicitly.

skills.title: State
skills.summary: Where UI state lives and choosing a state management approach

concepts.title: Lifting state up
concepts.summary: Moving shared state to the closest common parent so the components that need it stay in sync

variants.q: A product page has a `SizePicker` and a `PriceLabel` side by side. The price depends on the chosen size, and right now `SizePicker` keeps the size in its own local state. What is the usual fix?
choices: Have `PriceLabel` read the selected size from the picker's DOM
Move the size into their common parent's state and pass it to both
Keep a second copy of the size in `PriceLabel` and sync them with effects
Move every piece of the page's state into a global store
variants.explain: State belongs in the closest component that all of its readers share. A second copy synced by effects gives two sources of truth that drift, and a global store is more than two siblings need.

variants.q: When is local component state the right place for a value, rather than a shared or global store?
choices: Whenever the value is a boolean rather than an object
Never: all state should be global so it is easy to debug
When only it and its children use it, like a dropdown's open flag
Only for values that were fetched from the server
variants.explain: Keep state as close as possible to where it is used; a dropdown's open flag concerns nobody else. Fetched data usually belongs in a server-state cache rather than plain local state.

concepts.title: State in the URL
concepts.summary: Keeping shareable view state such as filters, sort order and page number in the query string

variants.q: A user filters a product list to "red, size M, page 3", copies the URL and sends it to a colleague, who sees the unfiltered first page. What is the fix?
choices: Save the filters in `localStorage` instead of component state
Show a message asking the colleague to set the filters again
Store the filters on the server in the user's session
Keep the filters and page in the URL query string
variants.explain: State that defines what's on screen, and should survive refresh, back/forward and sharing, belongs in the URL. `localStorage` and the session are per browser or per user, so the colleague still gets the default view.

variants.q: Which piece of state is the best candidate to keep in the URL?
choices: The selected tab on a settings page that users bookmark
The text of a comment the user is still typing
Whether a tooltip is currently showing
The open WebSocket connection for live updates
variants.explain: Bookmarkable, shareable view choices fit the URL. A tooltip's visibility is momentary, and drafts or live objects don't belong in a URL at all.

concepts.title: Immutable updates to signals
concepts.summary: Signals compare values by reference, so arrays and objects need a new value through `set` or `update`

choices: `push` doesn't work on an array held in a signal
`computed` only recalculates on the next change detection
Signals freeze arrays, so `push` fails silently
`set` got the same array reference, so the signal reports no change
variants.explain: A signal compares old and new values with `Object.is` by default; mutating and setting the same array looks unchanged, so dependents aren't notified. Use `this.items.update(list => [...list, 'new'])`.

variants.q: `user` is a `signal<User>`. Which update correctly changes `user.address.city`?
choices: `this.user().address.city = 'Oslo'`
`this.user.update(u => Object.assign(u, { address: { ...u.address, city: 'Oslo' } }))`
`this.user.update(u => ({ ...u, address: { ...u.address, city: 'Oslo' } }))`
`this.user.update(u => ({ ...u, city: 'Oslo' }))`
variants.explain: Each object on the path to the change needs a new copy, with untouched fields copied over. `Object.assign` onto `u` mutates and returns the same reference, so the signal sees no change.

concepts.title: Synchronous signal updates
concepts.summary: A signal write takes effect at once: later reads, including `computed()` values, see it before the view refreshes

choices: It depends on when change detection runs
variants.explain: Signal writes are synchronous, so each `count()` read sees the previous write and the value goes 1, 2, 3. The view still refreshes once, at the next change detection. `update(c => c + 1)` is the shorter way to write it.

choices: `0`: `computed` values refresh at the next change detection
`2`: reading `doubled` recalculates it from the new `count`
`1`: `computed` reads the value from before the update
`undefined` until the template has read `doubled` once
variants.explain: A `computed` is lazy: reading it after a dependency changed recalculates it on the spot, so it is never stale. It doesn't wait for change detection.

concepts.title: Server state caching
concepts.summary: Treating fetched data as a cache keyed by request (for example TanStack Query), separate from UI state

variants.q: A paged list fetches through a query cache. The cache key is `['todos']`, while the fetch function reads the current page. Switching pages shows the same todos every time. What's wrong?
choices: The fetch function must be declared outside the component
Query caches store only the first page by default
The page must be passed as a separate option, not in the key
The page is missing from the cache key
variants.explain: The key identifies the cached data, so anything the fetch depends on must be part of it. With `['todos', page]` each page gets its own entry, and changing the page triggers a fetch.

variants.q: Two components on screen at the same time ask a query cache for the key `['user', 42]`. How many requests does a library like TanStack Query make?
choices: Two, one per component that asks
One, shared by both components
None until one of them calls `refetch()`
One per change detection cycle in each component
variants.explain: Queries with the same key share one cache entry, so concurrent consumers are deduplicated into one fetch. That's a main reason to use a server-state cache instead of fetching separately in each component.

concepts.title: Dependency tracking in `computed` and `effect`
concepts.summary: Only signals read synchronously during a run become dependencies; reads in callbacks or untaken branches don't

choices: `setTimeout` copies the signal's value when it is scheduled
`query()` is read in a later callback, so the effect has no dependencies
Effects run once unless created with `{ manualCleanup: true }`
Signals can't be read from inside timer callbacks
variants.explain: Only reads made while the effect function itself runs are tracked. Here nothing is read synchronously, so nothing triggers a rerun. Read `const q = this.query()` first, then use `q` in the timeout.

variants.q:
`showName()` is `false` when `label` is first read. While it stays `false`, `name` changes. Is `label` recalculated?

```ts
label = computed(() => (this.showName() ? this.name() : 'Anonymous'));
```
choices: No: only signals read on the last run are dependencies
Yes: every signal mentioned in the function is a dependency
Yes, but only at the next change detection
No: `computed` never tracks signals inside a ternary
variants.explain: Dependencies are recorded per run. With `showName()` false, `name()` wasn't read, so changing it can't affect the result. Once `showName` becomes true, the next run reads and tracks `name`.

concepts.title: Service scope and shared state
concepts.summary: A service provided in `root` is one shared instance; listing it in a component's `providers` gives each instance its own copy

choices: Root services are created lazily, once per route
Signals inside services don't notify components
The badge needs `OnPush` to see changes from a service
`providers` gives the badge its own `CartService`, separate from the root one
variants.explain: Injection looks up the nearest provider, and the badge's own `providers` entry wins over `providedIn: 'root'`. Remove it so the badge shares the root instance.

variants.q: A dialog component lists `DraftService` in its `providers`, and its child components inject it. Two of these dialogs are open at once. Which instances exist?
choices: One, shared by both dialogs, since services are singletons
One per dialog, shared by that dialog's children
One per child component that injects it
One for the first dialog; the second one throws
variants.explain: A component-level provider creates an instance per component, and its descendants resolve to the nearest one. That's useful for state that belongs to one dialog, and a trap when the state should be shared.

skills.title: Performance
skills.summary: Measuring and improving page speed and Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, INP)

concepts.title: Core Web Vitals
concepts.summary: LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness) and CLS (visual stability), Google's user-experience metrics

variants.q: Users complain that text jumps down just as they tap it, because a banner image loads above it with no reserved space. Which Core Web Vital measures this?
choices: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
Time to First Byte (TTFB)
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
variants.explain: CLS measures unexpected movement of visible content. Giving images `width` and `height` (or an `aspect-ratio`) reserves the space and prevents the shift.

variants.q: Clicking "Add to cart" runs a 400 ms synchronous handler before the page visibly responds. Which Core Web Vital captures this?
choices: Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
First Contentful Paint (FCP)
variants.explain: INP measures the delay from a user interaction to the next frame being painted; it replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. LCP is about how fast the main content loads.

variants.q: A news page shows its headline image only after 4.5 seconds because the file is huge and loaded late. Which Core Web Vital reflects this?
choices: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
Total Blocking Time (TBT)
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
variants.explain: LCP times how long the largest visible element, often a hero image or headline, takes to render. Total Blocking Time is a lab metric related to main-thread work, not one of the three Core Web Vitals.

concepts.title: Lazy-loading images
concepts.summary: `loading="lazy"` defers offscreen images until they near the viewport; the image at the top should load eagerly

variants.q: A long article has 40 images, and only the first is visible when the page loads. Which markup is a good default for the images further down?
choices: ``
``
`` with no script
``
variants.explain: Native `loading="lazy"` lets the browser fetch an image only as it gets close to the viewport. `defer` and `async` are `<script>` attributes, and `data-src` without a script never loads at all.

variants.q: A team adds `loading="lazy"` to every image, including the large hero image at the top of the page. What usually happens to Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)?
choices: It improves, because fewer bytes are downloaded at first
It stays the same, since lazy loading only affects images below the fold
It gets worse, because the hero image starts downloading later
It can no longer be measured once lazy loading is on
variants.explain: The hero is usually the LCP element, and lazy-loading delays its download. Load images above the fold eagerly (optionally with `fetchpriority="high"`) and lazy-load the rest.

concepts.title: Lazy routes and `@defer`
concepts.summary: Splitting code with `loadComponent` routes and `@defer` blocks so it downloads only when needed

variants.q:
What does this route do to the app's bundles?

```ts
{
  path: 'reports',
  loadComponent: () => import('./reports/reports').then(m => m.Reports),
}
```
choices: Nothing: `loadComponent` only delays creating the component
It removes `Reports` from the production build
It preloads `Reports` in a web worker at startup
`Reports` moves to its own chunk, fetched when the route is first visited
variants.explain: A dynamic `import()` is a split point, so the component and code only it uses go into a separate chunk. Users who never open Reports never download it, as long as nothing else imports it statically.

choices: The chart's code is fetched and rendered once the placeholder scrolls into view
The chart renders immediately; only its data loads later
The chart's code stays in the main bundle but is hidden until visible
The chart renders only during server-side rendering
variants.explain: Dependencies used only inside `@defer` go into a separate chunk that loads when the trigger fires; `on viewport` watches the placeholder. Using `SalesChart` elsewhere in the same template would keep it in the main chunk.

variants.q: A dashboard's initial bundle is 2 MB, mostly from a charting library used only on one admin page. What's the most effective fix?
choices: Run the bundle through a second minifier pass
Lazy-load the admin page's route
Serve the bundle from a CDN closer to users
Switch the chart components to `OnPush` change detection
variants.explain: Splitting at the route keeps the library out of the code every user downloads. A CDN speeds delivery but still sends 2 MB, and `OnPush` affects rendering, not download size.

concepts.title: List virtualization
concepts.summary: Rendering only the rows in view for very long lists (for example the Angular CDK's virtual scroll viewport)

variants.q: A table renders 20,000 rows and scrolling is janky. What does virtualization change?
choices: It moves rendering of the rows into a web worker
It pages the data so only 50 rows are fetched
It keeps every row in the DOM but hides off-screen ones
It renders only rows near the viewport
variants.explain: Virtualization keeps the DOM small by mounting just the visible window plus a buffer. Hiding rows with CSS still leaves 20,000 nodes for the browser to manage.

variants.q: After virtualizing a long list, what is a known trade-off?
choices: Rows can no longer have their own click handlers
Find-in-page misses rows that aren't rendered
The list must be sorted on the server first
Every row must have the same length of text
variants.explain: Off-screen rows don't exist in the DOM, so Ctrl+F and some assistive technologies can't reach them. That's one reason to use virtualization only when the list is truly long.

concepts.title: Profiling with Angular DevTools
concepts.summary: Recording change detection in the Angular DevTools profiler to see which components were checked and how long each took

variants.q: You record an interaction in the Angular DevTools profiler. What does it show for each change detection cycle?
choices: The network requests the cycle triggered
The components and lifecycle hooks that ran, with time spent in each
The JavaScript heap size before and after the cycle
The page's Core Web Vitals scores for that moment
variants.explain: The profiler records each change detection cycle and breaks it down by component and hook, so you can see which ones are slow or checked more often than expected. Network and memory belong to the browser's own tools.

variants.q: Typing one letter in a search box produces a change detection cycle in which the profiler shows every component on the page being checked, though only the results list changed. What is a usual next step?
choices: Wrap the search box in a `@defer` block
Replace `@for` with the older `*ngFor` directive
Make components `OnPush` or signal-driven so unaffected subtrees are skipped
Move the results list into a web worker
variants.explain: Default change detection checks every component each cycle. `OnPush` components are checked only when an input reference changes, an event fires inside them, or a signal their template reads changes.

concepts.title: OnPush, pure pipes and references
concepts.summary: `OnPush` components and pure pipes rerun only when an input's reference changes, so mutating objects is missed

choices: The `user` reference didn't change, so the OnPush card isn't checked
`@Input` properties become read-only after the first binding
OnPush components only update their view in `ngOnInit`
Interpolation in an OnPush template is cached until reload
variants.explain: An OnPush component is checked when an input gets a new reference, an event fires inside it, or a signal it reads changes. Replace the object, `this.user = { ...this.user, name: 'Grace' }`, or hold it in a signal.

variants.q: `total` is a pipe with the default `pure: true`. After `this.items.push(newItem)`, what does `{{ items | total }}` show?
choices: The new total: pipes run on every change detection
The new total, but only if the component is `OnPush`
An error: pipes can't take arrays as input
The old total: a pure pipe reruns only when its input reference changes
variants.explain: Angular caches a pure pipe's result and calls it again only when an argument changes by reference (or a primitive changes value). Assign a new array, `this.items = [...this.items, newItem]`, to get a new total.

concepts.title: Layout thrashing
concepts.summary: Interleaving DOM reads and writes so the browser recalculates layout over and over

variants.q:
This loop is slow with many boxes. Why?

```ts
for (const box of boxes) {
  const h = box.offsetHeight
  box.style.height = `${h + 10}px`
}
```
choices: Template strings are slow inside hot loops
Each `style` write repaints the screen immediately
Each read after a write forces a layout
`for...of` is slower than a classic `for` loop
variants.explain: Reading a layout property makes the browser apply pending style changes first, so every iteration lays out the page again. Read all heights first, then write all styles.

variants.q: Which pattern avoids layout thrashing when resizing many elements?
choices: Do all reads first, then all writes
Alternate reads and writes inside one loop
Wrap each style write in its own `setTimeout`
Read with `getComputedStyle` instead of `offsetHeight`
variants.explain: Batching reads before writes means layout is computed once for the reads and once after the writes. `getComputedStyle` reads also force style and layout work, so swapping APIs doesn't help.

skills.title: Accessibility
skills.summary: UIs everyone can use, following WCAG

concepts.title: Native buttons over clickable divs
concepts.summary: Using `<button>` for actions so keyboard, focus and screen-reader support come built in

variants.q:
What do keyboard users lose with this control? ```html
Save
```
choices: Nothing, as long as it has a visible text label
Only the hover and active styles
Mouse clicks stop working on touch devices
Tab focus, Enter/Space, and the button role
variants.explain: A `div` has no role, no focusability and no keyboard activation. `<button type="button" (click)="save()">` provides all three for free.

variants.q: A team adds `role="button"` to a clickable `div`. What else is still needed for it to behave like a real button?
choices: Nothing: the role adds keyboard support
`tabindex="0"` plus Enter/Space handlers
Only an `aria-label` describing the action
Only a visible `:focus` outline style
variants.explain: ARIA roles change what assistive technology announces, not how the element behaves. You must add focusability and keyboard activation yourself, which is why a native `<button>` is the better choice.

variants.q: A page needs two controls: "Go to account settings" opens a different page, and "Delete draft" performs an action on the current page. Which markup is the right fit?
choices: An `<a href="#">` for both, with JavaScript deciding the action
An `<a href="/settings">` link and a `<button>`
Two `<button>` elements with `onclick` handlers
Two `<div role="link">` elements with click handlers
variants.explain: Links navigate and buttons act, and each brings the matching keyboard behaviour and announcement. A `div` with a role needs focus and key handling added by hand, and `href="#"` anchors announce a destination that doesn't exist.

concepts.title: Alt text
concepts.summary: Describing an image's purpose in `alt`, or using `alt=""` when it's purely decorative

variants.q: A decorative divider image adds nothing to the content. What should its `alt` attribute be?
choices: Leave `alt` off entirely
`alt="divider image"`
`alt="decorative"`
variants.explain: An empty `alt` marks the image as decorative and screen readers skip it. Leaving `alt` off is worse: many screen readers then read the file name.

variants.q: A link contains only a magnifying-glass icon image and goes to the search page. What is the best `alt` for the image?
choices: `alt="Search"`
`alt="magnifying glass icon"`
`alt="click here"`
variants.explain: When an image is a link's only content, its `alt` becomes the link's name, so it should say where the link goes or what it does. Describing the picture tells users nothing useful, and an empty `alt` leaves the link unnamed.

variants.q: An image is a bar chart showing revenue rising every quarter of the year, and nothing else on the page describes it. Which `alt` serves screen reader users best?
choices: `alt="Bar chart of the company's quarterly data"`
`alt=""`, because charts are visual content
`alt="Bar chart: revenue rose each quarter"`
`alt="revenue-chart-final-v2.png"`
variants.explain: A meaningful image needs alt text that carries its message when nothing nearby does. A file name or only the image type gives no information, and an empty alt tells assistive tech to skip content that matters.

concepts.title: Labelling form fields
concepts.summary: Associating every input with a `<label>`; a placeholder is not a label

variants.q: A form uses `<input placeholder="Email" />` with no label. What is the main accessibility problem?
choices: Placeholders aren't supported in every browser yet
The input can't receive keyboard focus at all
Screen readers always read placeholders twice
It has no dependable label once typing starts
variants.explain: A placeholder isn't a dependable label and it disappears while typing, which hurts screen reader users and anyone who forgets what the field was. Use a visible `<label>` tied to the input.

variants.q: Which markup correctly labels the input in a reactive form?
choices: `<label for="email">Email</label><input formControlName="email" />`
`<label for="email">Email</label><input id="email" formControlName="email" />`
`Email`
`<label id="email">Email</label><input formControlName="email" />` as siblings
variants.explain: A label's `for` must match the input's `id`. `formControlName` links the field to the form model, not to a label, and a sibling label without `for` isn't associated, whatever its own `id`.

concepts.title: Colour contrast
concepts.summary: WCAG AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text against its background

variants.q: Under WCAG 2 level AA, what is the minimum contrast ratio for normal-size body text?
variants.explain: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. 7:1 is the stricter AAA level.

variants.q: A design uses light grey `#999` text on white for form hints, which is below 3:1. What is the accessible fix?
choices: Make the hint text italic
Darken it to at least 4.5:1
Add a tooltip repeating the text
Increase the letter spacing
variants.explain: Contrast depends on colour, not style. Italics, spacing or tooltips don't make low-contrast text readable.

concepts.title: Testing with a screen reader
concepts.summary: Using VoiceOver, NVDA or TalkBack yourself to check that a page can be used without seeing it

concepts.title: Focus management in dialogs
concepts.summary: Moving focus into a modal when it opens, keeping it there, and returning it when it closes

variants.q: A custom modal opens, but keyboard focus stays on the button behind it, and Tab moves through the page underneath. What should happen instead?
choices: Focus stays on the opener so users don't lose their place
Focus moves to the browser's address bar
Into the dialog, trapped, back to the opener on close
Tab is disabled entirely until the dialog closes
variants.explain: Keyboard and screen reader users need to land in the dialog and not wander behind it, then come back where they were. The native `<dialog>` element opened with `showModal()` handles much of this.

variants.q: After a modal closes, focus jumps to the top of the page. Why is that a problem, and what's the fix?
choices: Users lose their place; return focus to the opener
It breaks browser history; call `history.back()` on close
It scrolls the page; disable page scrolling on close
It's fine: the top of the page is the expected target
variants.explain: Sending focus to the start forces keyboard users to tab all the way back. Restoring focus to the opener keeps them where they were.

concepts.title: Live regions (`aria-live`)
concepts.summary: Marking an area so screen readers announce content that changes without a page load, like a "Saved" message

variants.q: After clicking Save, a "Changes saved" message appears in a `<div>` at the top of the form. Sighted users notice it; screen-reader users hear nothing. What fixes it?
choices: Give the message `tabindex="0"` so it can be reached
Make the message text larger and bold so it stands out
Add `aria-hidden="true"` to the rest of the form
Put the text in an existing `role="status"` element
variants.explain: Screen readers announce changes inside a live region (`role="status"` is a polite one), and the region should exist before the text is inserted so the change is noticed. A tabindex makes it focusable but doesn't move focus or announce anything.

variants.q: What is the difference between `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-live="assertive"`?
choices: Polite waits until the screen reader finishes speaking; assertive interrupts it
Polite only works on buttons; assertive works on any element
Polite announces once; assertive repeats until it's dismissed
Polite is for visible text; assertive is for visually hidden text
variants.explain: Assertive is for urgent messages, such as an error that needs attention now. Most status updates should be polite, so they don't cut off what the user is listening to.

skills.title: Responsive design
skills.summary: Layouts that work on every screen size

concepts.title: Viewport meta tag
concepts.summary: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` so phones use the real screen width

variants.q: A page's media queries work in a resized desktop browser, but on phones it shows the desktop layout zoomed out. What is most likely missing?
choices: A `min-width` set on the `body` element
The viewport meta tag
A mobile stylesheet linked with `media="handheld"`
`box-sizing: border-box` on every element
variants.explain: Without the viewport tag, mobile browsers lay the page out at a wide virtual width (often around 980 px) and scale it down, so small-screen media queries never match.

variants.q: What does `width=device-width` in the viewport meta tag do?
choices: Sets layout width to the device width in CSS pixels
Locks the page to the device's physical pixel count
Disables pinch-to-zoom on the page for all users
Makes every image scale to the screen width
variants.explain: It makes the layout viewport as wide as the device's screen in CSS pixels, so CSS widths and media queries behave as expected. Physical pixels are a separate thing, handled through the device pixel ratio.

variants.q: A site's viewport tag is `width=device-width, initial-scale=1, user-scalable=no`. Why do accessibility audits flag it?
choices: It makes text render smaller than 16 px
It blocks screen readers from reading the page
It forces the page to a fixed desktop width
It stops people with low vision from pinch-zooming
variants.explain: Disabling scaling removes a basic way to enlarge content, which conflicts with WCAG's resize requirements. The width and initial-scale parts are the normal, recommended settings.

concepts.title: Mobile-first media queries
concepts.summary: Writing base styles for small screens and adding `min-width` queries as space grows

variants.q:
In a mobile-first stylesheet, how does a two-column layout for wider screens get added?

```css
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
```
choices: `@media (max-width: 768px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; } }`
`@media (orientation: portrait) { .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; } }`
`@media (min-width: 768px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; } }`
Override `.grid` with `!important` in a separate file
variants.explain: Mobile-first means the unqueried styles are for small screens, and `min-width` queries layer on changes for larger ones. A `max-width` query would apply two columns to small screens, the opposite of what's wanted.

variants.q: Why do many teams write mobile-first CSS rather than desktop-first?
choices: Browsers evaluate `min-width` queries faster
`max-width` media queries are deprecated
Mobile-first CSS doesn't need the viewport tag
Wider layouts are added, not undone
variants.explain: Starting simple and adding complexity for wider screens usually means fewer overrides. Desktop-first tends to require undoing layout rules for small screens. Neither approach removes the need for the viewport tag.

concepts.title: Responsive images with srcset and sizes
concepts.summary: Offering several image widths so the browser downloads the one that fits the layout and screen

variants.q: An image has `srcset="a-400.jpg 400w, a-800.jpg 800w, a-1600.jpg 1600w"` but no `sizes`. It is shown at 300 px wide in a sidebar. Why do phones and laptops often download the 1600 px file?
choices: `srcset` always picks the largest candidate available
Without `sizes`, it assumes `100vw`
The `w` descriptors are ignored when there's no `src`
Browsers only use `srcset` on slow mobile networks
variants.explain: With `w` descriptors, the browser needs `sizes` to know the rendered width; the default is `100vw`. Adding `sizes="300px"` (or a media-based list) lets it pick a smaller file.

variants.q: Two phones show the same image at 400 CSS pixels wide. One has a device pixel ratio of 1, the other 3. With `srcset` in `w` units and the right `sizes`, what happens?
choices: Both get the same file, since the CSS width matches
Only the first phone uses `srcset` at all
The DPR 3 phone picks a wider file
The DPR 3 phone gets the smallest file to save data
variants.explain: The browser multiplies the slot width by the device pixel ratio when choosing a candidate. That is the point of offering several widths: high-density screens get enough pixels without small screens overpaying.

concepts.title: Grid `auto-fit` with `minmax()`
concepts.summary: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))` fits as many columns as there's room for, without media queries

choices: The columns stay 200px wide and the grid scrolls sideways
Columns drop one by one as they'd fall under 200px
Nothing changes until a media query switches the layout
All the cards shrink evenly but stay in a single row
variants.explain: `auto-fit` creates as many tracks as fit at the 200px minimum, and `1fr` shares out the leftover space, so the column count falls as space shrinks: five columns at 1000px, one at 300px.

variants.q: A grid uses `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))` in a 1000px container but holds only two cards, which stretch to 500px each. What change keeps them about 200px wide, with empty space after them?
choices: Set `grid-auto-flow: dense`
Add `flex-wrap: wrap` to the grid
Switch `auto-fit` to `auto-fill`
Set `justify-items: stretch`
variants.explain: `auto-fill` keeps the empty tracks, so the two cards take two of five 200px columns. `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks to zero width, which lets `1fr` stretch the cards across the row.

concepts.title: Container queries
concepts.summary: Styling a component based on its container's size (`@container`) instead of the viewport's

variants.q: A card component should switch to a horizontal layout when it has 500 px of space, whether it's in a narrow sidebar or a wide main column. Which CSS feature fits this?
choices: Container queries
Viewport media queries
`@supports` feature queries
`clamp()` on the card's width
variants.explain: Media queries only know the viewport size, so the same card would get the same layout in both places. Container queries respond to the space the component actually has.

choices: `@container` must be nested inside an `@media` rule
The query must use `min-inline-size`, not `min-width`
The card needs `display: grid` for the query to apply
No ancestor has `container-type` set
variants.explain: A container query is evaluated against the nearest ancestor declared as a container. Without a `container-type`, there is no container to measure. `min-width` is valid in container queries.

concepts.title: Flex and grid items' automatic minimum size
concepts.summary: Flex and grid items won't shrink below their content by default; `min-width: 0` lets them

variants.q: In a `display: flex` row, the main column has `flex: 1` and contains a long URL with no spaces. On narrow screens the column overflows the page instead of shrinking. What's the usual fix?
choices: Set `flex-shrink: 2` on the main column
Set `min-width: 0` on the column
Set `width: 100%` on the main column
Switch the row to `display: inline-flex`
variants.explain: Flex items default to `min-width: auto`, which won't let them shrink below their content's minimum width. `min-width: 0` removes that floor; raising `flex-shrink` doesn't help while the floor is there.

variants.q: A grid uses `grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr`, and a wide `<pre>` block in the second column pushes the page wider than the screen. Which change keeps the column within the viewport?
choices: Use `grid-template-columns: 200px auto`
Add `overflow: visible` to the `<pre>`
Use `200px minmax(0, 1fr)`
Set `width: 100vw` on the grid container
variants.explain: `1fr` behaves like `minmax(auto, 1fr)`, so the track can't go below its content's minimum size. `minmax(0, 1fr)` allows it to shrink, and the `<pre>` can then scroll inside with `overflow: auto`.

skills.title: Frontend security
skills.summary: Preventing XSS and CSRF and handling sensitive data in the browser

concepts.title: Where to store auth tokens
concepts.summary: Tokens in `localStorage` are readable by any script on the page; `HttpOnly` cookies are not

variants.q: An app keeps its session token in `localStorage`. An attacker finds an XSS hole. What can their script do with the token?
choices: Nothing: `localStorage` is sandboxed from page scripts
Read it, but only if the token isn't encrypted
Use it only while the user's tab stays open
Read it and send it to the attacker's server
variants.explain: Any script on the origin can read `localStorage`. With an `HttpOnly` cookie the script can't read the token, though it can still make requests from the victim's page, so XSS remains serious.

variants.q: What does marking a session cookie `HttpOnly` protect against?
choices: Scripts reading the cookie's value
The cookie being sent over plain HTTP
Cross-site requests carrying the cookie
The server overwriting the cookie later
variants.explain: `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from `document.cookie` and other scripts. Sending only over HTTPS is the `Secure` flag, and cross-site sending is governed by `SameSite`.

variants.q: A site moves its session token from `localStorage` into an `HttpOnly` cookie. An XSS hole remains. Which statement is correct about what injected script can still do?
choices: It can copy the token, but only while the tab is in the background
It can still send requests as the user, but can't read the token
It can no longer do anything harmful, since the token is hidden
It can read the cookie through `document.cookie` after a reload
variants.explain: HttpOnly stops scripts from reading the token, so it can't be stolen and reused elsewhere, but the browser still attaches it to requests the injected script makes from the victim's page. XSS stays serious.

concepts.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
concepts.summary: Attacker-supplied input that ends up running as script in other users' browsers; escape output for where it goes

variants.q: A forum saves posts as typed and inserts them into the page as raw HTML. A user posts ``. What happens when others view the post?
choices: Nothing: browsers ignore event handlers inside user content
Only the poster's own browser runs the code
The broken image is hidden and the post shows as empty
The code runs in each viewer's browser as if it came from the forum
variants.explain: This is stored XSS: the markup is served as part of the forum's own page, so the browser runs it with the forum's origin. Escaping the text on output, or sanitising any HTML you allow, prevents it.

variants.q: What is the main defence against XSS when showing user-supplied text in a page?
choices: Escaping it for the context where it is inserted
Encrypting the text before saving it in the database
Serving the whole site over HTTPS only, with HSTS
Checking in the browser that the text has no `<script>` tag
variants.explain: Output escaping turns `<`, `>` and quotes into harmless entities, so the text is displayed instead of run; Angular interpolation does this by default. HTTPS and encryption don't change what the browser executes, and a `<script>` filter misses event-handler attributes.

concepts.title: XSS, `[innerHTML]` and `DomSanitizer`
concepts.summary: Angular escapes interpolated text and sanitizes `[innerHTML]`; `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` turns that protection off

variants.q:
A user's comment is ``. What happens when it's rendered with `

{{ comment }}

`?
choices: The image tag is created and the alert fires
It shows as text: interpolation escapes strings
Angular strips the tag and shows nothing
Angular throws an error on HTML inside strings
variants.explain: Interpolation sets text content, so the markup is displayed rather than parsed. Raw HTML only comes into play with `[innerHTML]` or direct DOM writes.

variants.q:
The same comment, ``, is bound with `
`. What happens?
choices: The alert fires: `[innerHTML]` inserts raw HTML as given
It shows as escaped text, exactly like interpolation
Angular sanitizes it: the `onerror` handler is removed, so no script runs
Angular refuses the binding and throws an error
variants.explain: Angular treats `[innerHTML]` values as untrusted and sanitizes them, keeping safe tags like `` but dropping event handlers; in development it warns that content was stripped.

variants.q: To keep some inline styles, a developer passes HTML rendered from user-written Markdown through `bypassSecurityTrustHtml` before binding it to `[innerHTML]`. What has this done?
choices: Turned off sanitizing for that value, so injected event handlers can run
Nothing risky: Angular still removes scripts from trusted values
Escaped the HTML so it is shown as plain text
Allowed styles only; handlers and scripts are still removed
variants.explain: The bypass methods tell Angular the value is already safe, so it is inserted untouched. Use them only for content you control; for user content, sanitize with an allow-list instead.

concepts.title: Content Security Policy
concepts.summary: A response header that limits where scripts and other resources may load from, as a second line against XSS

variants.q: A page sends `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'`. An attacker injects `<script>steal()</script>` into the HTML. What happens?
choices: It runs, because it comes from the same origin
It runs, but it can't make any network requests
The browser blocks the inline script
The server rejects the response before sending
variants.explain: With `script-src 'self'`, only scripts loaded from the page's own origin run; inline scripts need `'unsafe-inline'`, a nonce or a hash. CSP is enforced by the browser, not the server.

variants.q: A team adds `'unsafe-inline'` to `script-src` because an old analytics snippet broke under their new CSP. What has this done?
choices: Nothing important: it only affects the analytics snippet
It makes the policy apply only to inline scripts
It disables CSP for third-party scripts only
Injected inline scripts can run again
variants.explain: Allowing all inline script re-enables the most common XSS payload. Use a nonce or hash for the one snippet, or load it as an external file.

concepts.title: SameSite cookies and CSRF
concepts.summary: The `SameSite` cookie attribute controls whether cookies go on cross-site requests, limiting CSRF

variants.q: A bank's session cookie is set with `SameSite=Lax`. A malicious site auto-submits a hidden `POST` form to the bank's transfer endpoint. Is the cookie sent?
choices: Yes: `Lax` allows every top-level request
No: not on a cross-site `POST`
Yes, unless the cookie is also `HttpOnly`
No: `Lax` cookies are never sent cross-site
variants.explain: `Lax` sends the cookie on cross-site top-level navigations using safe methods like `GET`, but not on cross-site `POST`s or subresource requests. That blocks the classic form-post CSRF.

variants.q: A cookie is `SameSite=Lax`. A user clicks a link on another site to `https://app.example/delete?id=5`, and that endpoint deletes on `GET`. What happens?
choices: It isn't sent, so nothing is deleted
The browser asks the user to confirm first
It's sent, so the delete goes through
The request is blocked by CORS
variants.explain: `Lax` still sends cookies on top-level `GET` navigations, so state changes on `GET` stay exploitable. Keep `GET` safe and do changes with `POST`, `PUT` or `DELETE`.

concepts.title: `javascript:` URLs
concepts.summary: User-supplied links can carry `javascript:` URLs; Angular sanitizes bound URLs, but bypassing the sanitizer re-opens the hole

variants.q: A profile page renders `Website` with a value the user entered. What happens if they enter `javascript:alert(document.cookie)`?
choices: The script runs when someone clicks the link
Angular prefixes it with `unsafe:`, so clicking runs nothing
The browser refuses to render the link at all
Angular throws during change detection
variants.explain: Angular's URL sanitizer catches `javascript:` in bound URLs and prefixes it with `unsafe:`, with a warning in development. Still validate on input, so the link points somewhere useful.

variants.q: `url` holds a user-entered string. Which binding still lets a `javascript:` URL run when clicked?
choices: `<a [href]="url">`
`<a href="{{ url }}">`
`<a [href]="url.trim()">`
`<a [href]="sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustUrl(url)">`
variants.explain: Property bindings and interpolation both go through the URL sanitizer. `bypassSecurityTrustUrl` marks the value as safe, so Angular inserts it unchanged.

variants.q: What is the safest way to accept a user-provided URL for a link?
choices: Parse with `new URL()`; allow only http(s)
Strip the substring `javascript:` from the value
HTML-escape the value before putting it in `href`
Check that the value starts with `www.`
variants.explain: Allow-listing schemes after parsing handles casing, whitespace and encoding tricks. Stripping a substring is a deny-list that variants like `JaVaScRiPt:` or embedded tabs get around.
